title: Alpine loss dominated an endpoint share contrast, but change tests were uncertain in ten zooplankton tanks
abstract: We tested whether fish raised the share of supplied focal zooplankton by increasing focal counts or reducing alpine counts. We used ten mixed-community tanks from a public 2016 experiment. Final focal shares were 100% with fish and 91.80% without fish. An exact split of the pooled endpoint share difference assigned 8.00 percentage points to alpine loss and 0.60 to focal gain. Alpine loss made 93.0% of this contrast. The fish effect on change in focal count was +32.2 adults per 30 L, with a bootstrap interval of -114.0 to +163.6 and an exact p value of 0.706. All three planned change tests were uncertain after correction. Endpoint tests did not survive correction across six tests. Thus an endpoint share increase does not establish a net focal count gain. The source paper already showed species-specific predator effects; our contribution is a group-level split, exact inference and a source-cell audit. One released Bosmina count conflicts with a published absence claim. Ten tanks, one source lake per elevation, selected taxa and two visits limit inference. No thermal index or share of the field climate-tracking gap is estimated. Code, derived evidence, a figure, hashes and retrieval instructions are included.

display.caption: Each line is one tank. Fish and no-fish tanks received the same source assemblages. Both arms had large focal count gains. Alpine adults were not recorded at the end in any fish tank. The planned fish effect on focal count change was uncertain.
